questions.question_text:
A ranger compares the number of nests found in forest, grassland, wetland and dunes.
Which display is most suitable?

options.text: Column graph
Line graph
options.why: Joining habitat categories suggests continuous change between categories that have no time order.

options.text: Timeline
options.why: A timeline places events in time, but these data compare habitat categories.

options.text: Number line
options.why: A number line locates values but does not compare named habitat frequencies.

questions.solution_text: The habitats are categories, so separate columns make their counts easy to compare.

questions.question_text:
Scientists record a lake's depth on the first day of each month for a year.
Which display best shows the changing depth?

options.text: Line graph
Picture graph
options.why: Repeated symbols compare counts but do not show the month-to-month change clearly.

options.text: Unordered list
options.why: An unordered list removes the time sequence needed to see how depth changes.

options.text: Single column
options.why: One column can show only one value and cannot represent twelve monthly depths.

questions.solution_text: A line graph places the months in order and shows how depth changes across the year.

questions.question_text:
Butterfly sightings in four gardens are $14$, $22$, $30$ and $38$.
Which display best shows each garden's proportion of all sightings?

options.text: Sector graph
Line graph
options.why: This treats the garden categories as a continuous sequence instead of showing parts of a whole.

options.text: Dot plot
options.why: This shows the distribution of numerical values rather than each garden's share of the whole.

options.text: Stem-and-leaf plot
options.why: This groups numerical values by place value rather than showing category proportions.

questions.solution_text: Use a **sector graph** because its sectors show each garden's proportion of the whole.

questions.question_text:
A survey records the number of bees seen per visit: $5$ bees on $180$ visits, $6$ on $220$ visits and $7$ on $460$ visits.
Would a dot plot with one dot per visit be appropriate?

options.text: No, the frequencies require too many dots to draw and read easily.
Yes, because there are only three different bee counts.
options.why: This considers the number of distinct values but ignores the large number of dots required by their frequencies.

options.text: No, because bee counts are categorical data.
options.why: This mistakes discrete numerical counts for named categories.

options.text: Yes, because one dot can represent each different bee count.
options.why: This uses one dot per distinct value and loses the supplied frequencies.

questions.solution_text: The data are discrete numerical, but a dot plot with one dot per visit would require too many dots.

questions.question_text:
Reptile counts at Rock, Sand, Creek and Scrub sites are $13$, $21$, $16$ and $10$.
Why is a line graph inappropriate for comparing these site counts?

options.text: Joining named sites suggests meaningful values between categories.
Line graphs cannot display any numerical values.
options.why: This reverses the role of line graphs, which display numerical measurements.

options.text: All counts must be equal before a line graph can be used.
options.why: This invents an equality requirement; line graphs can show changing values.

options.text: A line graph can contain only two data points.
options.why: This invents a limit on the number of data points.

questions.solution_text: The sites are categories. Values halfway between their names have no meaning, so joining the counts with lines is inappropriate.

questions.question_text:
A pond's dragonfly counts over six consecutive weeks are $24$, $31$, $29$, $38$, $42$ and $36$.
Which display is most appropriate for showing change over time, and why?

options.text: Line graph, because it shows how the count changes over consecutive weeks.
Sector graph, because it shows the week-to-week changes.
options.why: This confuses showing proportions of a whole with showing change over time.

options.text: Stem-and-leaf plot, because it preserves the order of the weeks.
options.why: This mistakes ordering values by place value for preserving their time sequence.

options.text: Dot plot, because stacked dots show the order of the weeks.
options.why: This mistakes showing frequencies of values for showing when those values occurred.

questions.solution_text: Use a **line graph** because the purpose is to show change over consecutive weeks.
